words.definition: A compelling personal charm that inspires devotion and draws the attention of others.
words.example: The moment she walked on stage, her charisma drew every eye and hushed the crowd.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'car-is-ma' — a gleaming car everyone turns to stare at; it has pure magnetic pull.

words.definition: Having a magnetic charm that naturally attracts, captivates, and inspires people.
words.example: The charismatic coach could make even the benchwarmers believe they would win the championship.
words.mnemonic: Car + kiss + magnetic: a charismatic person magnetically pulls a whole crowd toward them.

words.definition: Fluent, persuasive, and graceful use of language when speaking or writing.
words.example: His eloquence at the funeral left no dry eye in the chapel.
words.mnemonic: 'Elo-' like a beautiful 'hello' + Latin 'loqui' (to speak): speaking so well it moves people.

words.definition: To hold the seat of authority and direct a meeting, ceremony, or organization.
words.example: The retired judge was asked to preside over the town's annual debate.
words.mnemonic: PRE + SIDE: you sit at the premier side — the head seat — to run the whole meeting.

words.definition: A person who manages and carefully protects another's property, affairs, or resources.
words.example: As steward of the estate, he kept every acre thriving while the owners traveled abroad.
words.mnemonic: STY + WARD: a keeper who WARDs (guards) the pig STY — he guards whatever is entrusted to him.

words.definition: To rub or smear with oil, often as part of a sacred or ceremonial act.
words.example: The archbishop stepped forward to anoint the new king with holy oil.
words.mnemonic: Think 'an ointment' rubbed on: to anoint is to dab oil on someone in ceremony.

words.definition: To officially make someone a priest, or to decree something by formal authority.
words.example: The church will ordain three new priests at Sunday's ceremony.
words.mnemonic: ORDER + -dain: an authority issues an ORDER that makes the appointment official.

words.definition: Famous, respected, and highly regarded within a particular profession or field.
words.example: An eminent cardiologist flew in to consult on the senator's rare condition.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'Eminem went' — everybody knows Eminem; being eminent means everybody knows and admires you.

words.definition: Surpassing all others; ranked as the very best in a particular area.
words.example: For decades she remained the preeminent authority on ancient Greek pottery.
words.mnemonic: PRE- (above) stacked on top of 'eminent': standing above even the already-distinguished ones.

words.definition: Widely admired and celebrated for remarkable achievements or a distinguished record.
words.example: The general capped his illustrious career with a medal from the president.
words.mnemonic: Shares 'lustr-' with 'lustre': an illustrious name has a shining, glowing reputation.

words.definition: Asserting harsh control over others in an arrogant, bossy, and overbearing manner.
words.example: Her domineering manager rewrote every email and forbade any decision without his approval.
words.mnemonic: Picture a DOMINO toppling everyone into line — a domineering person forces his will on all.

words.definition: Unpleasantly overpowering in attitude, pushing to control everyone around oneself.
words.example: His overbearing mother-in-law criticized the wedding plans until the couple stopped answering her calls.
words.mnemonic: OVER + BEARING: like a huge bear bearing down ON you — far too pushy and heavy-handed.

words.definition: Showing great authority and commanding respect, sometimes in a bossy, dictatorial way.
words.example: With a magisterial wave of his hand, the conductor silenced the entire orchestra.
words.mnemonic: From 'magistrate' and 'master': acting like a master judge whose word is final.

words.definition: A government or system of rule, especially a strict or authoritarian one.
words.example: Under the new regime, newspapers were censored and public protests were banned.
words.mnemonic: 'Reg-' as in regal and reign — a regime is the reigning set of rulers in charge.

words.definition: A messenger or official representative sent to deal with another government.
words.example: The president dispatched a special envoy to negotiate the ceasefire.
words.mnemonic: ENVOY sounds like 'on a voyage' — someone sent on a voyage to represent you abroad.

words.definition: A person sent to represent a group or carry out a special mission on its behalf.
words.example: The king dispatched an emissary to negotiate peace with the rival court.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'emit' — an emissary is emitted, sent outward, to deliver a message.

words.definition: Someone or something authorized to act, stand in, or vote for another.
words.example: Unable to attend the shareholder meeting, she voted by proxy through her lawyer.
words.mnemonic: 'Proxy' ≈ 'approximately you' — a near stand-in acting in your place.

words.definition: The front position of an advancing group, or the leaders of a new trend.
words.example: These sculptors were the vanguard of a movement that redefined modern art.
words.mnemonic: 'Van' = front (the van of a convoy) + 'guard' — the front guard leading the way.

words.definition: A leader in name only, holding a title but wielding no real authority.
words.example: The aging monarch became a mere figurehead while the ministers ran the country.
words.mnemonic: The carved 'figure' on a ship's 'head' (prow) — decorative, leads nothing, just for show.

words.definition: A highly respected person who inspires others within a particular field.
words.example: Physicists from around the globe gathered to honor the field's greatest luminary.
words.mnemonic: Root 'lumen' = light — a luminary shines, an intellectual star lighting the way.

words.definition: A perfect example of a particular quality; a model of excellence.
words.example: She was held up as a paragon of honesty, never telling even a small lie.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'paired gem' — the flawless gem every other is compared against.

words.definition: A person or thing serving as a typical or ideal model to copy.
words.example: This cathedral is often cited as the finest exemplar of Gothic architecture.
words.mnemonic: Contains 'example' — an exemplar is the example worth copying.

words.definition: An experienced, trusted adviser who guides and trains a less experienced person.
words.example: Her graduate mentor spent hours teaching her how to design careful experiments.
words.mnemonic: From Mentor, the wise guide of young Telemachus in Homer's Odyssey.

words.definition: A person who supports, sponsors, or financially backs an artist, cause, or business.
words.example: The wealthy patron funded the young composer's studies and his first symphony.
words.mnemonic: Root 'pater' = father — a patron acts like a supportive father, funding you.

words.definition: A person who gives money or kind assistance to someone or a cause.
words.example: An anonymous benefactor paid the hospital bills of every child on the ward.
words.mnemonic: 'Bene' = good + 'factor' = doer — a benefactor is a 'good-doer.'

words.definition: A person responsible for guarding, maintaining, or taking care of something.
words.example: As custodian of the archive, he protected centuries-old manuscripts from damage.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'custody' — a custodian keeps something in their custody.

words.definition: A person who watches over and directs the work of others.
words.example: The plantation overseer monitored every worker and reported to the owner.
words.mnemonic: One who 'sees over' everyone — 'oversee' plus the doer ending '-er.'

words.definition: A person with authority to judge disputes or decide what is acceptable.
words.example: The committee became the final arbiter of which films deserved the award.
words.mnemonic: Shares a root with 'arbitrate' — an arbiter arbitrates, settling fights.

words.definition: Clever and skillful, especially in handling tricky situations or using the hands.
words.example: She gave an adroit reply that defused the argument without offending anyone.
words.mnemonic: French 'à droite' = to the right; right-handedness was prized as skill — adroit.

words.definition: Shrewd, careful, and clever, especially in business or practical matters.
words.example: A canny investor, she sold her shares just before the market collapsed.
words.mnemonic: Think of a thrifty Scot who always 'can' spot the smart move and save a penny.

words.definition: A secret and cunning plot designed to cause harm or gain advantage.
words.example: The duke's machinations toppled two rivals before anyone suspected he was behind it.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'machine' + 'nation' — picture a shadowy machine cranking out evil plots behind the nation's back.

words.definition: Secret plotting or scheming, usually to gain power or achieve a hidden purpose.
words.example: The royal court seethed with intrigue, every courtier whispering plans against the others.
words.mnemonic: In + 'trigue' (sounds like 'league') — a secret league working in the shadows.

words.definition: To control or influence someone cleverly, often unfairly, for your own benefit.
words.example: She manipulated her coworkers into doing her tasks by faking helplessness.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'manus' (hand) — you handle people like puppets on strings.

words.definition: To persuade someone to do something using flattery or clever deception.
words.example: He inveigled his way into the exclusive club by flattering the doorman shamelessly.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'in-a-veil' — you lure someone in while hidden behind a veil of sweet talk.

words.definition: To attract someone by offering something tempting or pleasurable.
words.example: The smell of fresh bread enticed passersby into the little bakery.
words.mnemonic: 'En-TICE' → 'in twice' — a treat so good it pulls you in a second time.

words.definition: To charm or trick someone with pleasing but misleading behavior.
words.example: The con artist beguiled the widow with his warm smile and false promises.
words.mnemonic: Be + 'guile' (cunning) — to be full of guile toward someone while charming them.

words.definition: To combine several things into one stronger, more unified whole.
words.example: After the merger, the company consolidated its three offices into a single headquarters.
words.mnemonic: Con + 'solid' — you make something solid by pressing scattered parts together.

words.definition: Polite respect and willingness to yield to another's wishes or judgment.
words.example: Out of deference to the elderly professor, the students let him speak first.
words.mnemonic: Related to 'defer' — when you defer to someone, you bow to them out of respect.

words.definition: A gesture or attitude of respectful submission, such as a deep bow.
words.example: The servants made a deep obeisance as the emperor entered the hall.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'obey' + 'stance' — the bowing stance you take to obey a ruler.

words.definition: A serious, dignified manner that naturally commands respect.
words.example: The judge spoke with such gravitas that the noisy courtroom fell instantly silent.
words.mnemonic: From 'gravity' — a person with gravitas carries a weighty, grave presence.

words.definition: The power or influence to affect people, events, or decisions.
words.example: With her political clout, the senator pushed the bill through in days.
words.mnemonic: A 'clout' is also a heavy blow — someone with clout can hit hard and get results.

words.definition: A position of dominant power or controlling influence over others.
words.example: The rebel faction gained ascendancy after the old regime collapsed.
words.mnemonic: From 'ascend' — you climb to the top and rule over everyone below.

words.definition: The state of being first in rank, importance, or order.
words.example: The doctor stressed the primacy of prevention over expensive later treatment.
words.mnemonic: From 'prime/primary' — being number one, the first and foremost.

words.definition: The state of being highest in authority, rank, or power.
words.example: For centuries the navy secured the nation's supremacy over the seas.
words.mnemonic: From 'supreme' — sitting at the absolute top, above all others.

words.definition: To be the strongest, most common, or most noticeable element.
words.example: In the desert flora, hardy cacti predominate over softer, thirstier plants.
words.mnemonic: Pre + 'dominate' — to stand out as the main, ruling presence in a scene.

words.definition: The period during which a monarch or ruler holds power over a land.
words.example: Under Queen Victoria's reign, the British empire stretched across every continent.
words.mnemonic: REIGN sounds like RAIN — imagine a ruler's authority pouring down over the whole kingdom.

words.definition: To organize and gather people or resources into proper order for a purpose.
words.example: She marshaled the volunteers into small teams before the storm hit the coast.
words.mnemonic: Picture a MARSHAL, the army officer, lining up the troops in neat rows.

words.definition: To gather or summon troops, support, or one's own inner strength.
words.example: He finally mustered enough courage to ask his boss for a raise.
words.mnemonic: MUSTER sounds like 'MUST' — you MUST pull everything together to face the moment.

words.definition: To plan and coordinate a complex activity carefully to produce a desired result.
words.example: The manager orchestrated the product launch down to the last press release.
words.mnemonic: Like the conductor of an ORCHESTRA, cueing every instrument so they all fit together.

words.definition: To lead or drive forward an effort, campaign, or movement from the front.
words.example: A teenage activist spearheaded the drive to clean up the polluted river.
words.mnemonic: The SPEAR's HEAD is the sharp point that strikes first — the one out in front leading.

words.definition: To give someone the authority or confidence to take control and act.
words.example: The new training program empowered employees to make decisions without waiting for approval.
words.mnemonic: EM- (to put in) + POWER — literally to put power into someone.

words.definition: Intense and passionate feeling or burning enthusiasm for something.
words.example: The crowd sang the national anthem with a fervor that gave me chills.
words.mnemonic: FERVOR sounds like 'FEVER' — a burning heat of emotion running through you.

words.definition: Great energy and eager devotion directed toward a cause or goal.
words.example: She pursued her new fitness plan with such zeal that friends worried she'd burn out.
words.mnemonic: ZEAL rhymes with 'PEEL' — peel away everything else and only burning enthusiasm is left.

words.definition: Warm, intense passion or eager enthusiasm.
words.example: He spoke of his homeland with an ardor that silenced the whole room.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'ardere,' to burn — think of glowing embers; ARDOR is a warmth that burns inside.

words.definition: Impossible to defeat, subdue, or discourage.
words.example: Despite three failed businesses, her indomitable spirit kept her trying again.
words.mnemonic: IN- (not) + Latin 'domitare' (to tame) — a wild thing that simply cannot be tamed.

words.definition: Inspiring fear or respect through being powerful, large, or impressive.
words.example: The chess champion proved a formidable opponent no challenger expected to beat.
words.mnemonic: From Latin 'formido' (fear) — something so imposing it fills you with dread.

words.definition: Deserving great respect or fear, especially as an opponent.
words.example: The old general remained a redoubtable figure long after he retired.
words.mnemonic: RE-DOUBT-able — an opponent so tough it makes you DOUBT you can ever win.

words.definition: To bully or pressure someone using stern words and harsh looks.
words.example: The lawyer tried to browbeat the witness into changing her story on the stand.
words.mnemonic: Lower your BROW into a scowl and BEAT someone down with intimidation.

words.definition: To hold and use a weapon, tool, or influence effectively.
words.example: The senator wields enormous influence over how the committee votes.
words.mnemonic: WIELD rhymes with 'SHIELD' — picture a knight who wields a sword and raises a shield.

words.definition: To announce or put into effect a law, decree, or idea officially.
words.example: The new government promulgated a decree banning single-use plastics nationwide.
words.mnemonic: Sounds like 'PROMO' + 'GATE' — open the gate and promote the announcement to everyone.

words.definition: To give a visible or concrete form to an abstract idea, quality, or feeling.
words.example: The old nurse seemed to embody kindness itself, soothing every frightened patient on the ward.
words.mnemonic: em + BODY — you put an idea into a BODY, giving a thought real flesh and shape.

words.definition: Lower in rank, power, or importance than someone or something else.
words.example: As a new recruit, he was subordinate to nearly every officer on the base.
words.mnemonic: sub- (under) + ordinate (ordered) — you are ordered UNDER someone above you.

words.definition: Willing to go along with rules, requests, or the wishes of others.
words.example: The compliant puppy sat the instant its owner raised a hand.
words.mnemonic: com-PLY — to ply is to bend; a compliant person bends to every command.

words.definition: Easy to teach, manage, or control, offering little resistance.
words.example: The docile old horse let the children climb all over its back without a fuss.
words.mnemonic: Same Latin root as 'doctor/doctrine' (docere, to teach) — a docile creature is easy to teach.

words.definition: Able to be pressed or bent into a new shape, or easily influenced.
words.example: Gold is so malleable that a jeweler can hammer it into paper-thin sheets.
words.mnemonic: MALLEable sounds like MALLET — a mallet hammers soft metal into any shape.

words.definition: To soften a firm stance and finally give in after resisting.
words.example: After hours of her begging, her father finally relented and let her go to the concert.
words.mnemonic: Hidden 'lent' from Latin lentus (soft, slow) — to go soft again and ease up.
